questions.question: Explain how the periodic table encodes electron structure, and translate in both directions: the configuration 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4, and the position period 2, group 1.
questions.expected_answer: The table orders elements by atomic number — proton count — and its geometry encodes electron structure twice over. The period number equals the number of energy levels the electrons occupy, and the group tracks the valence electrons: groups 1 and 2 hold one and two, and for groups 13 to 18 the units digit gives the count, so group 16 holds six and group 18 a full eight. Translating configuration to position: 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p4 uses three energy levels, so period 3, and holds six valence electrons — the 3s2 3p4 — so group 16: the element is sulphur. Translating position to configuration: period 2, group 1 means two levels and one valence electron — 1s2 2s1 — which is lithium. Position and configuration are two spellings of the same fact, and the transition metals sit between the two main-group blocks as a single family of hard, dense metals.

questions.question: State the four periodic trends with their directions, and show how the single tug-of-war picture explains all of them, including why fluorine is the strongest electron-puller.
questions.expected_answer: The four trends: atomic radius decreases across a period and increases down a group; ionisation energy increases across and decreases down; electron affinity strengthens across, with the halogens accepting electrons most readily; electronegativity rises across and falls down, with the noble gases sitting out because they rarely bond. The one picture: the nucleus hauls on the outer electrons like a tug-of-war team on a rope. Crossing a period adds protons — more pullers — while the outer electrons stay on the same level — same rope length — so the grip tightens: atoms shrink, electrons cost more to remove, and the atom drags harder on shared and incoming electrons. Descending a group adds a whole new level — a longer rope — with more inner electrons screening the pull, so the grip weakens: atoms grow, electrons leave cheaply, and the tug fades. Fluorine sits where both effects favour pulling — top right, a short rope with a relatively large team and almost no screening — making it the strongest electron-puller in chemistry, while the giant bottom-left metals barely hold their outer electron at all.

questions.question: Give the group portraits of the alkali metals, alkaline earth metals, halogens and noble gases: electron counts, ion charges, reactivity directions with reasons, and one everyday connection each.
questions.expected_answer: Group 1, alkali metals: one valence electron, cheap to lose, so the most reactive metals — soft, stored under oil, fizzing and even flaming in water, leaving alkaline solutions; they form plus-one ions, and reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron sits further out, better screened, on a longer rope. Group 2, alkaline earth metals: two valence electrons and plus-two ions; reactive but calmer, since losing two electrons costs more than one — magnesium burns with a white flare, and calcium compounds build cement, bones and teeth. Group 17, halogens: seven valence electrons, one short of full, so the most reactive non-metals, forming minus-one ions; reactivity decreases down the group — fluorine, small and unscreened, seizes electrons ferociously while iodine barely bothers — mirroring the metals' downward increase. Group 18, noble gases: full outer levels, nothing to lose or gain, chemically inert and existing as single atoms — filling party balloons and glowing signs — and serving as the arrangement every ion and bond in chemistry is trying to reach.
